speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel it is unnecessary for me to speak for more than a few moments in closing this debate. I may say that it comes as -a relief to me to have the opportunity to close the debate, because it has taken a long time.
The discussion has covered a wide range, and has been a valuable one. But it must be remembered that time is running on, and that before we get this emergency legislation through we have to consider a wide range of matters. I am in hopes that the house will make as rapid progress as possible in the days and weeks to come.
I am not at all sure that it is necessary for me to say anything about the position of the various parties with respect to the measure now before us. The principle of the measure was clearly expressed this afternoon by my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). It is, I submit, summed up in the last recital in the preamble of the bill, which is as follows:
And whereas it is necessary by reason of the existing national emergency that certain orders and regulations of the governor in council made under the War Measures Act and the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945 be
continued in force temporarily notwithstanding the expiry of the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act, 1945, in order to ensure an orderly transition from war to peace.
That is the principle of the bill; and I am surprised that any party in the house, any member in the house, should have found it necessary to take a position in opposition to the measure. I am surprised that that should be the case. It seems to me it is a measure which should pass unanimously, which should pass promptly. It seems to me the house should devote itself to considering, in as much detail as it wishes, orders in council which are appended to the bill. I should hope that that consideration would not be too detailed because, as has been pointed out, these orders in council are now the law of the land, have been for many years the law of the land, and are all destined to expire before very long. And so the degree of care required in legislation which is to be permanent is not required in legislation of this type.
Inevitably discussion has centred around certain of the orders in council which are appended to the bill. Those are the orders in council relating to controls. The positions of the three parties in this house with reference to controls has been carefully and repeatedly stated.
I have a feeling that those hon. members who took such an adamant and uncompromising position against the continuation of con-trois_I have an idea, I say, that those members have weakened very much in the last few weeks.
The Progressive Conservative opposition apparently came to the house determined to agitate for the removal of controls and the reduction of taxation, thinking those were the two things that the people of the country- or at least a great many of them-wanted.^ I am not saying anything about the reduction of taxation, because, of course, that is not within my province or department. But the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), in his first speech in the session, stated definitely and positively the position of the Progressive Conservative party on controls. I venture to say that today the leader of the Progressive Conservative party would not state that position in those terms. He would not take that position now.
The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) has stated positively he is for the abolition of all controls. And we can go throughout that party, here and there, and remember the speeches which have reverberated through this chamber, talking about the cancellation of controls, condemning the government for holding on to controls, stating that we must do away with them-and at
Emergency Powers

once-and that we cannot retreat gradually, stating that an orderly or gradual retreat is inevitably disorderly, and that the only way to get rid of controls is to get rid of them.
That has been the position taken by prominent and official members of the Progressive Conservative party throughout all this session-until recently; until they went home during the Easter recess, and found out something. They found out what was the sentiment of the people in their constituencies.
Nothing is more humourous, it seems to me, than the report of the deliberations of the convention or the annual meeting-or whatever it is called-of the Progressive Conservative party. According to the reports, the party divided into two elements. One was for doing away with controls and the other was for perpetuating some controls. Finally they decided, as I read in the Globe and Mail, to compromise by recommending that all controls be abolished which would retard the production of building materials. That was the momentous decision on the subject of controls arrived at by the Progressive Conservative convention.
The position I have stated on behalf of the government is a clear one. It is that we must get out of this field as soon as it is safe to do so, and I mean safe from the point of view of the people of this country. I have stated repeatedly that I cannot go along with the C.C.F. position, which apparently contemplates the indefinite continuation of controls. We cannot possibly contemplate a position like that, because we have no constitutional power to do so. We cannot have price controls by dominion authority permanently in this country.
The dominion government has to get out of price controls sooner or later. The dominion government must lay its plans so as to get out of price controls on an orderly, gradual and safe basis. That is the position of the Liberal party today; that is the position of the government, and I think it is the only common sense position that any party can take in this house. Recently a big smoke-screen was thrown up in connection with this whole matter of controls, and we have had such speeches as that delivered by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) about the courts and about certain powers which the wartime prices and trade board has the right to confer upon the sugar corporation and so on. Some of his points may be very good. I do not know whether those are or not.	.
As I said in my opening speech with regard to these controls, the powers are extensive. They had to be extensive. We pared down

some of them and perhaps some of them should be taken out in committee, but to elevate individual sections in long orders to the level of the principle of the bill and present them as the reason why the Conservative party is going to vote against this bill is to show a lamentable and shocking lack of proportion and confuses the issue entirely.
I am not going to say very much more about this. Nearly everybody has expressed himself and I have expressed myself already on two or three occasions. This attitude of handing everything back to business, which the Conservative party started out to put before this house as their attitude and their policy is impracticable, is dangerous and is wrong in the light of present conditions. It has been modified since by sheer opportunism. Reaction tempered by opportunism is the principle that underlies the attitude taken by the Progressive Conservative party in this debate and in this vote.

desperate over there.

Mr. Chairman, I think I should say something to the committee about the government's plan with regard to considering this measure. It is proposed to take up section 1 first, the section we are on. My submission would be that the rules of order, whatever the practice has been, should be

applied in the consideration of that section, and I hope that the discussion of it would be short. With regard to section 2, section 2 must be amended if amendments are to be made to any of the orders in council in the schedule, and so I will propose that section 2 stand until the schedule is dealt with. If amendments to any of the orders in council, or sections of the orders in council, are passed by the house, then it will be necessary to go back to section 2, which would have stood, and amend it so as to give effect to these amendments to the orders in council. Then I think that, before we deal with the orders in council in the schedule, we might as well deal witl) the remaining sections of the bill. And so the course of procedure I propose is to take section 1, let section 2 stand, take sections 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, then the schedule, and then go back to section 2 and amend it as way be required by any amendments to the schedule.
